A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DMM research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization and protocol revisions.

before.justification: v1 Section 6 and Appendix D report original FEMNIST and Stack Overflow next-word prediction experiments, including accuracy and client computation/communication results.

after.justification: v2 reports experiments on both benchmarks, revised efficiency results, and additional training-accuracy trajectories in Appendix D.

M1.justification: Protocol 1 changes from sharing fresh inputs to the next committee and releasing outputs through SecAgg to sharing within the current committee and reconstructing combined shares directly at the server. The parity-check, commitment and random-linear-check machinery in v1 Appendix C is removed. v2 Section 4 also introduces a prefix-sum optimization that reshares only noise instead of both gradients and noise.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same FEMNIST handwritten-character classification and Stack Overflow next-word prediction tasks with the same described datasets and populations. Stack Overflow was already evaluated in v1 Appendix D; its promotion to the main text adds no coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds naive secret resharing as a communication-cost comparator in both efficiency tables. DDG, Flamingo/SecAgg and central Honaker comparisons remain. v2 explicitly labels the central optimal comparator BandMF; v1 inconsistently references multi-epoch and banded factorization, so that relabeling alone does not establish a new comparator.

E3.justification: FEMNIST optimal/Honaker training lengths change from 765/512 to 1445/1024 iterations, with Honaker separation b changing from 85 to 64. Stack Overflow changes from 1500/1024 iterations with b=85 to 2052/2048 with b=342/512. Efficiency reporting changes from full-protocol last-round costs to LRP penultimate-round costs, on different hardware.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix D adds training trajectories across privacy levels and both factorizations for both datasets (Figures 5–6), supplementing the existing final-accuracy comparisons. Section 4 also reports a preliminary, unquantified finding that Skellam noise performed worse than discrete Gaussian noise.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly states that efficiency values average ten runs; v2 omits this averaging and run-count information. This establishes a reporting removal, not fewer actual runs. Neither version provides confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty bands for the accuracy curves.

E6.justification: Both accuracy-versus-privacy plots are replaced under revised training schedules, with Stack Overflow results now showing closer agreement with central-DP methods. Efficiency values change substantially: v1 Table 2 reports Honaker costs of 17.3 seconds and 50.1 MB for ΠPPFL, whereas v2 Table 1 reports 412 milliseconds and 25.1 MB for LRP. Naive-resharing costs and training trajectories add further results. Changed components, hardware and schedules prevent treating these as same-setting improvements.

T1.justification: Appendix C replaces the security theorem and proof using SecAgg/commitment functionalities and parity checks with a simulation proof tracking additive errors through resharing and direct reconstruction. Reconstruction coefficients now explicitly depend on the participating subset. The principal DP and accuracy bounds and their Appendix B derivations are substantially retained.

C1.justification: The central claims of distributed matrix-mechanism privacy, constant-overhead resharing and dropout tolerance remain. v2 strengthens the introduction's comparison from utility close to central DP to matching central DP, and explicitly claims less than ten seconds of additional client computation. Replacing 'local DP' with 'distributed DP' clarifies the terminology for the existing threat model.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about privacy degradation from corrupted or dropped clients, explains the central-DP accuracy gap through discretization, modular clipping and discrete-noise aggregation, and discusses alternative noise mechanisms' applicability. v1 Appendix E's detailed masking-attack discussion is removed, while encryption-based alternatives are reconsidered through concurrent work rather than left simply as an open direction.

D1.justification: The reported hardware changes from an Ubuntu/Intel Xeon machine with 192 GiB memory to an AMD EPYC 7R32 processor and A10G GPU. v2 newly specifies δ=1/N in the accuracy captions and describes server-routed authenticated channels using a PKI. Dataset splits, model architectures and most optimization hyperparameters are retained, often relocated to Appendix D.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning through discussion of Ball et al.'s concurrent encryption-based stateful aggregation, including claimed communication, computation and malicious-security tradeoffs. It adds Skellam, Poisson-binomial, newer central-DP and fluid-MPC literature, while pruning the earlier secure-aggregation survey. These changes extend beyond bibliographic or citation-style updates.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, contributions are enumerated, and DP, security-model and secret-sharing preliminaries are reorganized ahead of the method. Experimental descriptions are redistributed between the main text and Appendix D. Protocol terminology changes throughout, and v2 adds a conclusion, acknowledgements and impact statement.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Protocol diagrams and captions are revised, accuracy plots are redrawn with different ranges and styling, and Stack Overflow displays move into the main text. Efficiency tables add a naive-resharing column and change protocol labels; two new training-trajectory figures appear in the appendix.

improvement.justification: v2 improves clarity and critical context through explicit security assumptions, consistent distributed-DP terminology, naive-resharing comparisons, training curves and privacy qualifications. The gain is limited by removal of ten-run averaging information and an inconsistent new abort condition: Protocol 1 checks for too few dropped clients, whereas Appendix C checks for too few remaining clients. Changed hardware and evaluation settings also prevent interpreting lower timings as controlled performance gains.
